The Story of Harishen Chakravartin

I bow to Lord Jina, whose eye is omniscience, and I write the story of Harishen Chakravartin.

King Sinhdhvaj of the famous city of Kampilya in Angadesh had a queen named Vapra. The hero of this story, Harishen, was their son. Harishen was intelligent, handsome, and very radiant. Everyone honoured him greatly.

Harishen's mother was righteous. She had unwavering faith in the Lord. This was why she always had Lord Jina's chariot taken out during the festival of Athaai and celebrated the occasion. Sinhdhvaj's second queen, Lakshmimati, had no faith in Jain dharma. She always reviled it. Once she said to her lord, 'My dear, today let my Brahmaji's chariot go through the city first — please give such an order.' Sinhdhvaj, without considering the consequences, agreed to Lakshmimati's request. But when the dharma-loving Queen Vapra learned of this, she was greatly distressed. She immediately took a vow: 'I shall eat only when my chariot goes out first.' Truly, the dharma is the refuge of the noble; their run is only toward dharma.

Harishen came to eat. Seeing his mother not smiling as usual but with a sad face, he was very sorry. When he learned the cause of her sorrow, he did not stay there even a moment longer and left the house. From there he went to a village of thieves. Seeing him, a parrot — trained by the thieves — said to its masters, 'Look, this prince is going. Catch him. You will gain.' But none of the thieves paid attention to the parrot's words. So Harishen passed through without any trouble. Truly, from the company of the wicked comes wickedness. And from such beings, no one ever receives any benefit.

From there, Harishen went to the ashram of an ascetic named Shatamanyu. There too was a parrot, but this one was not wicked like the first. Seeing Harishen, it thought, 'One whose face has radiance and beauty must certainly have virtues. This person going by must be some such soul.' Then it said to its masters, the ascetics, 'That prince is going. Please honour him.' The prince was greatly surprised. He had seen the first parrot's behaviour and now saw this one's.

The ascetics honoured Harishen and gave him guidance. He continued his journey and eventually became a great king. He ruled with justice and compassion, following the path of dharma. He honoured Jain monks, gave generously to the worthy, and protected his subjects. In time, he became a Chakravartin, conquering all directions. But despite all his worldly power, he never forgot his mother's devotion to dharma. He continued to honour Jain dharma throughout his reign and ultimately took initiation as a monk, attaining liberation.

This story teaches the importance of good company and the power of a parrot's words. The first parrot, trained by thieves, tried to harm Harishen, but its words were ignored. The second parrot, living with ascetics, recognised Harishen's virtues and recommended him for honour. The wise should seek the company of the good and avoid the company of the wicked, for company shapes character and destiny.
